newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Claridge to make new investments via Koor.
newsitem.headline: Claridge to make new investments via Koor.

text.p: Claridge Israel expects to use Koor Industries Ltd for all new investment it makes and may transfer some of its current holdings into Koor as well, Claridge president Jonathan Kolber said on Wednesday, a day after acquiring a 10 percent stake in Koor.
"If we exercise the option ... we'd like to have Koor become our main investment vehicle for all new investments," Kolber told Reuters.

Claridge, which is controlled by Canada's Charles Bronfman, acquired 10 percent of Koor from a California investment company, Shamrock Holdings Ltd, in a deal announced on Tuesday. Koor is Israel's largest holding company.
Claridge holds a 90-day option to buy another 10 percent, which would give it the remainder of Shamrock's Koor holding.
Kolber vehemently denied newspaper reports that he would be replacing Koor's president and chief operating officer, Benny Gaon.
"Not true, not true, not true," he said about the reports, adding that he wanted Gaon to stay and that it had not yet been decided who would act as chairman. Gold currently chairs Koors board.
"I can honestly tell you that someone from Claridge will be chairman...but Benny will stay on as CEO," Kolber said. He said he did not anticipate a clash between top executives.

Gaon, who brought Koor from the brink of bankruptcy in the early 1990s and then engineered a series of strategic partnerships for Koor-held companies, came under implicit criticism from Gold in recent weeks.

Citing Koor's lacklustre share price performance since Shamrock acquired its 20 percent stake in the holding company in early 1995, Gold said he wanted to spin off Koor's main publicly traded subsidiaries to shareholders.
Kolber said he was not sure he would adapt Gold's plan but indicated that there would be major changes at Koor once Claridge has raised its stake to 20 percent.

"I think some holdings should be sold, others should be merged and others need international partners," he said. "We have lots and lots of ideas." He stressed, however, that they were tentative and did not constitute a fully formed strategic plan.
If it exercises the option, Claridge will become Koor's second-largest shareholder. Koor's biggest shareholder, Bank Hapoalim, is limited under banking regulations from exercising its full rights.

Claridge paid approximately $185 million for its 10 percent holding, or $24.25 per American depositary share (ADS), which represented about a 10 percent premium over Koor's market price. Claridge can exercise its option at the same price.
"The first tranche we're paying with cash. If we go higher, we may borrow" he said.

Koor shares rose sharply in the days before the announcement of the sale on Tuesday on the back of huge off-the-floor transactions in Koor. On Tuesday, Claridge confirmed it had made the purchases, equally to nearly another two percent of Koor's equity.
Kolber reiterated his statement from Tuesday that the purchases were made to "test the market" but declined to elaborate.
Prior to the run-up, Koor ADSs had closed at about $20.80 last Friday, which would put the premium Claridge paid at nearly 17 percent.
Koor ADSs were trading at $22 in New York in late afternoon on Wednesday.
Kolber said the negotiations for the sale, which came at Claridge's initiative, began last week. He indicated feelers had been put out before then.

Kolber said Israel's anti-trust authorities have approved the transaction in principle but have attached certain conditions depending on its final details. He would not detail them but said it was likely officials would require certain divestitures.
Koor's principal interests are in telecommunications/electronics, agrochemicals and building products. Koor and Claridge both hold stakes in Israeli energy companies.
($1 = 3.51 shekels)
- David Rosenberg, Jerusalem newsroom, 972-3-537-0502 DER BSB
